questions.q: Which block is required by azurerm_kubernetes_cluster and defines the worker nodes pods schedule onto?
options: network_profile
default_node_pool
site_config
admin_ssh_key
questions.explain: default_node_pool is a required block on azurerm_kubernetes_cluster; it defines the initial set of worker nodes, including node_count and vm_size.

questions.q: What does setting identity { type = "SystemAssigned" } on an AKS cluster accomplish?
options: It assigns a static public IP address to the cluster
It gives the cluster its own Azure AD identity so it can manage supporting resources like load balancers and disks without a stored credential
It enables role-based access control inside Kubernetes itself
It disables the Azure control plane's billing
questions.explain: A system-assigned managed identity lets AKS create and manage Azure resources (load balancers, managed disks, scale sets) on your behalf without a long-lived credential in the configuration.

questions.q: Who manages and bills for the AKS control plane versus the node pool's VMs?
options: Both are managed and billed identically as a single unit
Azure manages the control plane; the node pool's VMs are the compute you size and pay for separately
The node pool's VMs are managed by Azure; the control plane is self-hosted
Neither is billed -- AKS is entirely free
questions.explain: AKS's control plane is a managed Azure service; the default_node_pool's VMs are the compute resources whose size (vm_size) and count (node_count) you configure and pay for.

questions.q: What does network_plugin = "azure" in the network_profile block give pods?
options: No networking at all -- pods must be manually assigned IPs
Real IP addresses from the VNet's address space, rather than an overlay network
Access to the public internet by default
A separate, isolated Kubernetes-only network with no connection to Azure resources
questions.explain: The azure (CNI) network plugin assigns pods real IP addresses drawn from the VNet, letting other Azure resources reach them directly, unlike an overlay network.

questions.q: After terraform apply successfully creates the AKS cluster, what is the next step to start deploying workloads onto it?
options: Run terraform destroy and recreate the cluster
Edit the azurerm_kubernetes_cluster resource block directly from kubectl
Use az aks get-credentials to retrieve the kubeconfig, then use kubectl to manage what runs inside the cluster
Nothing further is needed -- Terraform deploys containers automatically
questions.explain: Terraform's responsibility ends at provisioning the cluster. az aks get-credentials retrieves the kubeconfig so kubectl (or a CI/CD pipeline) can then deploy and manage workloads.
